passage: At the forest kindergarten outside Gothenburg, Diego, five, stomped over to Ulla. "It's not fair! Lars took my stick!" "You sound really upset. What do you want?" "My stick back! And he shouldn't grab." "Can you tell him that?" Diego marched back, arms stiff. "That's my stick. Ask first, please." Lars held it out and muttered, "Sorry."

qa.q: What did Diego say Lars took?
qa.a: His stick.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling as he stomped over to Ulla?
qa.a: Angry and wronged, and probably hoping Ulla would fix it. His stiff arms suggest he was holding a lot in.

qa.q: How did Ulla guide Diego?
qa.a: Ulla listened, asked what he wanted, and encouraged him to tell Lars himself.

qa.q: How might Lars see Diego marching back?
qa.a: Possibly surprised or embarrassed, though he handed the stick over. He may not have known the stick mattered so much.

grounding: Shows a preschooler complaining that it is not fair and being guided to say what he wants.

passage: In the school reading corner, Parul, six, held a book against her chest. "Harish Sir, it's not fair! Riya has the big cushion every day!" Harish sat down beside her. "You'd like the big cushion today?" "Yes. And she never shares." "Shall we make a turn list?" "With my name first?" "In order. Today Riya, tomorrow you." Parul frowned, then nodded and wrote a P on the sheet.

qa.q: What did Parul hold against her chest?
qa.a: A book.

qa.q: What does Parul's "And she never shares" suggest she feels?
qa.a: Left out and frustrated. The words may be exaggerated in the moment.

qa.q: How could Harish teach Parul a better way to object?
qa.a: Ask what she wants and propose a turn list, so the complaint becomes a fair plan.

qa.q: How might Riya see the turn list?
qa.a: Perhaps relieved to know the rule, or a little disappointed to lose her regular cushion.

grounding: Shows a preschooler objecting loudly that it is not fair and a teacher guiding her to state what she wants.

passage: I'm Tenzin, Dhruv's big sister. At tea time Mummy cut the cake, and Dhruv shouted, “It's not fair! My piece is smaller!” He banged the table. Mummy didn't tell him to stop complaining. She said, “You think it's not fair. What do you want?” Dhruv thought, still cross. “The same size as Didi.” Mummy put both pieces side by side. Mine was a bit bigger. She cut a sliver off mine and gave it to him. I didn't mind much. Dhruv stopped banging and ate.

qa.q: What did Dhruv bang?
qa.a: The table.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he shouted “It's not fair!”?
qa.a: He felt cross and hard done by, believing his piece was smaller. Tenzin could see the complaint was really a call for help.

qa.q: How did Mummy help Dhruv object in a better way?
qa.a: She listened and asked what he wanted, so he could say “the same size as Didi” instead of just shouting.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel about giving up a sliver?
qa.a: Tenzin didn't mind much, seeing it made things fair.

grounding: A sister observes a preschooler complain it's not fair, and their mother listens and helps him say what he wants.

passage:
Monday: “Papa! He took mine!” Vijay ran in yelling. His friend had his car. Harish knelt. “What do you want to happen?” “My car back!” “Can you tell him that?”
Wednesday: They practised. Harish played the friend. Vijay said, “I want my car back, please.” Harish handed it over.
Friday: At the park, a boy grabbed Vijay's bucket. Vijay said, “I want my bucket back, please.” The boy gave it. Vijay ran to Harish, beaming. “I said it myself!”

qa.q: What did the boy grab at the park on Friday?
qa.a: Vijay's bucket.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he ran in yelling on Monday?
qa.a: He was angry and upset that his friend took his car, and wanted his father to fix it.

qa.q: What did Harish do that taught Vijay a better way to object?
qa.a: He listened, asked what Vijay wanted, and practised the words with him so he could say it himself.

qa.q: How might Harish feel when Vijay runs to him beaming?
qa.a: He likely feels proud that Vijay has learned to speak up clearly.

grounding: Over a week, a father listens to his preschooler's complaints and guides him to state what he wants.

passage: It was raining, so the whole class crowded under the shelter, where there was only one swing. A girl had been on it a long time. Yusuf stamped over to Parul Ma'am. “It's not fair! She's had it forever!” Parul listened. “You've been waiting a long time and you're fed up. What do you want?” “A turn!” “Can you ask her? Try: ‘Can I have a turn after ten pushes?’” Yusuf went back and said it. The girl nodded. Yusuf counted the pushes loudly.

qa.q: How many pushes did Yusuf ask the girl to have before his turn?
qa.a: Ten pushes.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he stamped over to Parul Ma'am?
qa.a: He was frustrated and impatient after waiting a long time, and felt it was unfair.

qa.q: Which step by Parul Ma'am worked, and why?
qa.a: She named his feeling and gave him clear words to ask for a turn, which worked better than just complaining.

qa.q: How might the girl on the swing see Yusuf's request?
qa.a: She'd likely find it fair and easy to agree to, because he asked kindly with a clear number.

grounding: On a crowded rainy day, a preschooler complains “It's not fair!” and his teacher guides him to state what he wants.

passage:
In the colony sandpit, Manoj stamped his foot. "It's not fair! He took mine!" He pointed at a bigger boy digging with a yellow spade.

Dilnaz Didi came over from the bench. "You sound really upset. Tell me what happened."

"I put it down for one second, and he grabbed it!"

"And what do you want?"

"I want it back."

"Can you tell him that? Try: 'I was using that. Can I have it back?' I'll stand with you."

Manoj walked over, Didi behind him. "I was using that spade. Can I have it back, please?"

The boy shrugged and handed it over.

qa.q: What colour was the spade?
qa.a: Yellow.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he stamped his foot and shouted "It's not fair!"?
qa.a: He was most likely angry and frustrated that his spade was grabbed, and his loud complaint was really a call for help. He may also have felt a little small next to the bigger boy.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz Didi teach Manoj a better way to object?
qa.a: She listened, asked what he wanted, gave him simple words to say, and stood with him while he said them himself.

qa.q: How might the bigger boy see the situation?
qa.a: He might have thought the spade was free because it was put down, so a clear request made it easy for him to give it back.

grounding: It shows a preschooler complaining loudly that something isn't fair and an adult listening and guiding him to state what he wants.
